title: Wetlands give more to us than we realize
summary: Wetlands provide all kinds of benefits, writes Julia Anna Moore: locking away carbon, filtering water, providing a habitat for wildlife and protecting against storm surge. And they're also ideal places to simply pause and reflect, so visit one, she writes.
content:
by Julia Anna Moore, Maryland Matters May 3, 2025

by Julia Anna Moore, Maryland Matters May 3, 2025

The Eastern Shore is known for its beaches, but an often overlooked gem of the coast are the wetlands. They are fascinatingly one of the youngest geographical features on the planet, most  only between 6,000 and 10,000 years old, which is a blink compared to the rest of Earth’s  history.

Although the wetlands just got here, they have locked tons of ancient carbon into their sediment  and plants, and they’re still doing work as our emissions continue to grow. They have tons of  other benefits, like filtering our water, providing a place for fisheries to continue their life cycle,  and acting as a soaking buffer when the storm surge rises.

Wetlands also attract biodiversity, which  underpins human health and nutrition, and we all know health is true wealth.

Unfortunately, the space that wetlands occupy is on the decline, globally decreasing between 3%  and 7% each year. This is due to human impact, such as development on wetlands, but also the ever-rising sea levels pushing them inland. Wetlands may be able to survive if they are able to  migrate inland, but with human development impeding their movement, they are becoming  fragmented and eventually can die.

When wetlands die, their work stops, which exacerbates climate change issues.

Maryland as a state has a rich maritime heritage, and is affected by its water bodies, like the  Chesapeake, the Pocomoke and the Atlantic. The blue crab is an icon, beautiful to look at and  culturally significant to eat and protect. For a place that finds the water to be significant,  wetlands need to be a part of that narrative.

There is hope, with many initiatives that would allow these ecosystems to thrive far into the  future, but we have to lean into it as a society and focus on policy that will benefit generations  long after we are gone. We have to reshape how we think of these wetlands, because with the  inevitable future of sea level rise and climate change, they could save our beloved coasts.

Chances are there is a wetland right in your backyard or around the corner.

If you sit silently in a wetland, you’ll start to discover all of its secrets and how much life it  holds while we humans are busy. Small terrapins poking their heads out of the water, soaking up  the sun. A bald eagle soaring overhead, searching for the next fish to catch. Sunlight hitting the  puddles of water through the loblolly pines. Horseshoe crabs crawling up banks to take a rest from the tides. Cordgrass swaying in the wind as the hairs on your arms pick up on the change in  direction.

If we grow to understand these places, and love them, we will want to protect them. So on your  next free weekend, choose to visit one of your local Maryland wetlands.
